newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: India reaffirms call for total nuclear disarmament.
newsitem.headline: India reaffirms call for total nuclear disarmament.

text.p: India reaffirmed its hard line at the Conference on Disarmament on Thursday, pressing the established nuclear powers to make elimination of their weapon stocks an agreed aim when negotiating other nuclear arms issues.

The call for a fixed date for total nuclear disarmament is rejected by the major powers, which want wide agreements to prevent the spread of nuclear arms while keeping the future of their existing arsenals for negotiations within the club.
In her first address to the U.N.-sponsored forum this year, Indian ambassador Arundhati Ghose also expressed support for a "pragmatic, phased approach" towards a global ban on landmines.
The approach -- like that of neighbouring China -- should take into account the security concerns of states who use mines for "defensive purposes against enemy forces", she added.

Western states have accused non-aligned states led by India and Pakistan of blocking progress in the 61-member body this year by making their demands for talks on total nuclear disarmament a price for agreement on other issues.
Ghose said India backs starting negotiations to halt production of plutonium and highly-enriched uranium -- the fissile material used for making nuclear bombs -- but as part of an overall scheme.
"Nuclear disarmament remains our primary objective and our priority," she declared.
"India remains convinced that a fissile material cut-off treaty can be a useful and necessary step, but as part and parcel of a negotiated, phased programme for the elimination of nuclear weapons."

"We realise that a step-by step approach is necessary, but we are also convinced, that if progress towards nuclear disarmament is genuine, these steps must take place within a reasonable and specified time-frame," Ghose said.
The five declared nuclear weapon states, Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States, have opposed efforts by the non-aligned to launch talks on total nuclear disarmament.
They argue that Washington and Moscow must continue to negotiate bilateral reductions in their huge nuclear stockpiles before widening the process to include other powers.
Australia on Wednesday formally proposed appointing a "special co-ordinator" to try to hammer out a consensus on a Conference mandate for negotiations on landmines.
Britain's envoy Sir Michael Weston informed the Geneva body of the new Labour government's pledge on Wednesday to destroy Britain's anti-personnel landmines by the year 2005.
He read out Prime Minister Tony Blair's statement to Parliament and one by the secretary of state vowing to redouble efforts in Geneva to "get the main export countries to stop selling landmines".
"The United Kingdom continues strongly to support the immediate establishment of an ad hoc committee on anti-personnel landmines with a negotiating mandate," he said in a speech.
Weston, speaking to reporters, said: "I am quite optimistic that we will make the first step here shortly appointing a special co-ordinator. I think there is a good chance."

Mexico has stymied efforts to launch Geneva negotiations on a global ban on landmines, but the United States has been pressing its southern neighbour to go along with a consensus to appoint a special co-ordinator, according to Western diplomats.
China's envoy Sha Zukang told reporters: "We need to discuss mines to see how far we can go. We are all of different views.
"Some say total ban, some say phased ban. For the time being, China's position is clear -- we can't accept a total ban.
"China has long land borders. We need landmines for security and protection," Sha said.

China and Russia -- major producers and users of landmines -- are not part of Canada's "Ottawa Process" aimed at reaching a ban among 50 countries by December. This means that a viable, universal ban could only be clinched in Geneva, diplomats say.

John Holum, director of the U.S. arms control and disarmament agency, said last week that Washington would not sign any accord which emerged from the Canadian initiative on landmines as key states were not expected to be covered by it.
